# Across the Channel: Investigating Diel Dynamics (ACIDD)

Across the Channel: Investigating Diel Dynamics (ACIDD) was a student-driven research expedition in the Santa Barbara Channel, where I served as co-Principal Investigator and Chief Scientist. Our original goal was to investigate the daily rhythms of marine microbial communities, examining how their activity and physiology change over 24-hour light–dark cycles. With ship time awarded through the [UC Ship Funds program](https://scripps.ucsd.edu/ships/uc-ship-funds-program), we spent a year assembling a collaborative team, developing our sampling strategy, and preparing to lead an oceanographic expedition.

Just days before our cruise, the Thomas Fire erupted in Southern California, eventually becoming one of the largest wildfires in California's recorded history at the time. Rather than abandon our original objectives, we adapted our sampling plans to investigate how wildfire ash deposition might affect coastal marine ecosystems. This unexpected opportunity allowed us to collect observations and conduct experiments during an active wildfire event, contributing to early investigations of the effects of wildfire-derived aerosols on marine microbial communities.

These early observations also helped motivate my later research on how wildfire-derived organic matter influences marine microbial communities, explored in [Smoke on the Water](https://nbaetge.github.io/Smoke_on_the_water.html).

## Outreach and Media

ACIDD also became an opportunity to explore how science and art can work together to communicate ocean research. Through the vision of [Dr. Kelsey Bisson](https://science.nasa.gov/people/kelsey-bisson/) and support from a Keck Futures Initiative grant, we collaborated with artists and musicians to translate our scientific experiences into creative works.

The resulting [science–art collaboration](https://tos.org/oceanography/article/california-wildfire-burns-boundaries-between-science-and-art)  included illustrations, music, and a short film featured at the Environmental Film Festival in Washington, D.C. These projects offered new ways to share the experience of oceanographic fieldwork and engage audiences with the connections between wildfires, marine ecosystems, and environmental change.

Explore [Migrations Magazine](https://issuu.com/migrationsmag/docs/finalmigrationszinepages), which showcases our science–art collaboration.
